corpus.signal_text:
Trump’s “Mega Deal” in Venezuela Could Deepen Risks for Investors
Without meaningful democratic reforms, the agreement may jeopardize the investments Washington hopes to attract
Late on Friday night, Donald Trump announced what he called “the biggest oil deal in world history.” Under the terms described publicly so far, the US would obtain a controlling interest in a new venture involving 17 Venezuelan oil fields containing more than 65 billion barrels of proven reserves, with an effective 55 percent share of production and preferential access to crude at cost. The Trump administration says the arrangement could mobilize around $100 billion in private investment and eventually generate more than $200 billion in Venezuelan tax revenues. Much about the deal, including its precise legal structure, remains unclear.
There is nothing inherently objectionable about American companies making money from Venezuelan oil. Venezuela desperately needs foreign capital, technology and markets. PDVSA cannot rebuild the industry on its own, and reconnecting Venezuela to the American energy system would be preferable to another generation of dependence on Russia, China or Iran.
The problem is not that Washington wants investment. The problem is that it seems determined to make that investment possible without first solving the political and institutional problem that made Venezuela uninvestable in the first place.
Recalculating
The original expectation after Nicolás Maduro’s removal seemed straightforward enough. American oil majors would pour tens of billions of dollars into the country and restore production. Nine days after Maduro was captured, Trump gathered oil executives at the White House and invited them back to Venezuela. ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods responded with an inconvenient assessment: under the existing legal and commercial conditions, the country remained “uninvestable.” ConocoPhillips was interested but similarly cautious. Chevron, which never fully left, has continued expanding and is now preparing another significant restructuring of its Venezuelan operations. So far, the broad stampede of supermajors Washington appeared to expect has not come.
So Washington widened the search. Delcy Rodríguez traveled to India in June to court energy investment and deepen ties with Reliance and other Indian companies, in a trip conducted with remarkably explicit American encouragement. corpus.title: Oil, the most sensitive issue in Venezuelan politics
corpus.signal_text:
Oil, the most sensitive issue in Venezuelan politics
The agreement announced by Donald Trump has sparked widespread unease in a country with a deeply rooted sense of ownership over its natural resources
The oil agreements announced by U.S. President Donald Trump and Venezuela’s acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, of which only fragmentary details have so far emerged, have touched on some of the most sensitive areas of Venezuelan public debate: the relationship between oil, the state and citizens.
The existence of long-term agreements (at least 25 years), announced by a foreign president, with no verifiable details about their potential benefits and amid widespread suspicions about how the United States has used Venezuela’s national revenues in recent months, has sparked broad discontent. This unease has been only partly tempered by the instinct among certain local elites not to antagonize Washington, perhaps because they see Washington as the last remaining hope for a return to democracy. These agreements have not been submitted to Venezuela’s National Assembly, as required by the Constitution.
The debate over the exploitation and use of oil resources in Venezuela is more than a century old, dating back to the discovery of the country’s first oil fields. Over the decades, a powerful sense of ownership over oil wealth took root in Venezuelan society. In local political debate, commitment to national ownership of crude oil has long been regarded as a moral measure of political actors. Some of the most important works of Venezuelan political thought, such as Venezuela, Politics and Oil by Rómulo Betancourt (1956), place oil production and the strategy for developing it within a framework of national sovereignty at the center of their argument.
The dictatorship of Juan Vicente Gómez (1908-1935) has been judged harshly by Venezuelan historians for the lenient terms under which it negotiated the country’s first oil concessions with foreign companies, to the detriment of the national interest. Under Gómez, multinational oil firms established themselves in Venezuela and stayed for as long as possible.
Since then, each successive government has sought to strengthen national control over oil and its production, a longstanding goal of Venezuelan politics. The reform-minded and moderate administration of Isaías Medina Angarita (1941-1945) enacted the Hydrocarbons Law, which for the first time required multinational oil companies to operate under state regulations.
